explanations.explanation: Right at the gate, baker. God says, "Stand in the gate of the house of the LORD and proclaim this message…" (Jeremiah 7:2). Anybody coming in to worship has to pass through there. That's prime real estate for a message.

The treasury is a good guess for a temple spot, but it's not what the verse says. God tells Jeremiah to stand "in the gate of the house of the LORD" (Jeremiah 7:2). Out front, where everybody coming in can hear him. Nobody's getting a message in a treasury unless they're counting something.

A storeroom would be a quiet place to proclaim a message, and nobody would hear it. That's the opposite of the plan! God says to stand "in the gate of the house of the LORD" (Jeremiah 7:2). That's the spot where all the people of Judah come through.
Yes, baker. God says, "Correct your ways and deeds, and I will let you live in this place." (Jeremiah 7:3). He puts the way forward right at the start of the message. That's a door held wide open.

This one is true, so the card has it right. The text says, "Correct your ways and deeds, and I will let you live in this place." (Jeremiah 7:3). God starts the message with the way forward. Don't let the stern tone later on hide that.

That's it. God spells out the deceptive words: "This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD." (Jeremiah 7:4). Same line, three times. I think they were hoping the repeating would make it hold more weight.

An army is a classic thing to trust in, but that's not what God names here. The deceptive words are about a building: "This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD." (Jeremiah 7:4). Nothing about soldiers in this warning.

The king's riches don't come up in this warning. God points to a different set of words: "This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD." (Jeremiah 7:4). They were leaning hard on the temple itself.

You've got it, friend. God says, "if you act justly toward one another…" (Jeremiah 7:5). He's talking about how they treat each other, not just where they stand on Sunday. The list that follows gets even more specific.

explanations.answer: Bringing more sacrifices to the temple
explanations.explanation: More sacrifices sounds like a safe bet, but it's not on God's list here. The first thing He names is, "if you act justly toward one another…" (Jeremiah 7:5). He's after how they live with each other. Bringing more of the same wasn't what He asked for.

explanations.answer: Repeating the prayers of their fathers
explanations.explanation: Repeating prayers isn't what God names first. He says, "if you act justly toward one another…" (Jeremiah 7:5). The focus is on how people treat each other. Words alone were the problem He'd just warned about.

Careful, this one flips what God says. He doesn't offer a deal where they keep other gods and just treat people kindly. He says to correct their ways, "if you no longer oppress the foreigner and the fatherless and the widow, and if you no longer shed innocent blood in this place or follow other gods to your own harm…" (Jeremiah 7:6). Following other gods is on the list of things to stop.

Right, baker. God doesn't say they can keep following other gods. He lists it right alongside the rest: "if you no longer oppress the foreigner and the fatherless and the widow, and if you no longer shed innocent blood in this place or follow other gods to your own harm…" (Jeremiah 7:6). It's a package, not a pick-and-choose.

explanations.answer: They're delivered so they can keep going
explanations.explanation: Yep. God has them saying, "We are delivered, so we can continue with all these abominations" (Jeremiah 7:10). Read that slowly. They're treating the temple like a get-out-of-trouble card, and then going right back to it. God holds up that picture and asks if it makes sense.

explanations.answer: They're sorry and ready to change
explanations.explanation: I wish that was the line, friend. But sorry and ready to change is the opposite of what God quotes. He has them saying, "We are delivered, so we can continue with all these abominations" (Jeremiah 7:10). They're planning to keep going.

explanations.answer: They're poor and need His help
explanations.explanation: Needing His help would be a different conversation entirely. What God quotes is, "We are delivered, so we can continue with all these abominations" (Jeremiah 7:10). They're saying they're safe and they can carry on. Nothing in the verse about being poor.

That's the one. God asks, "Has this house, which bears My Name, become a den of robbers in your sight?" (Jeremiah 7:11). Then He adds, "Yes, I too have seen it…" A robbers' den is where people hide out after the damage is done, and that's the picture He chooses.

Lions have a den, sure, but that's not the picture here. God asks, "Has this house, which bears My Name, become a den of robbers in your sight?" (Jeremiah 7:11). It's robbers who hide out there, not lions.

A nest of vipers is a scary picture, but it's not the one God uses. He asks, "Has this house, which bears My Name, become a den of robbers in your sight?" (Jeremiah 7:11). Robbers, not snakes. The whole point is people treating His house like a hideout.

Yes, baker. God tells them to go to Shiloh and "see what I did to it because of the wickedness of My people Israel." (Jeremiah 7:12). He names the reason Himself. It's right there in the verse, so we don't have to guess.

Not quite, friend. God does give a reason for what He did to Shiloh. He says, "see what I did to it because of the wickedness of My people Israel." (Jeremiah 7:12). The reason is stated right in the verse.

Not this time, baker. God says the opposite: "I have spoken to you again and again but you would not listen, and I have called to you but you would not answer" (Jeremiah 7:13). That's a lot more than once. He kept speaking and calling.

Right. God says, "I have spoken to you again and again but you would not listen, and I have called to you but you would not answer" (Jeremiah 7:13). Again and again, plus calling on top of it. He kept reaching out to them.

That's it, friend. God says, "what I did to Shiloh I will now do to the house that bears My Name, the house in which you trust…" (Jeremiah 7:14). The very place they were leaning on is the place He's talking about. I think that stings.

The army doesn't show up in this verse. God says, "what I did to Shiloh I will now do to the house that bears My Name, the house in which you trust…" (Jeremiah 7:14). The thing they trust in is the house.

The king isn't who God names here. He says, "what I did to Shiloh I will now do to the house that bears My Name, the house in which you trust…" (Jeremiah 7:14). It's the house, the one they kept pointing to.

explanations.answer: Cast them out of His presence
explanations.explanation: That's what He says, baker. "And I will cast you out of My presence, just as I have cast out all your brothers, all the descendants of Ephraim." (Jeremiah 7:15). This is a heavy line, and it's okay to let it sit for a second. Then keep going, because there's more to hear.

Egypt isn't mentioned in this passage. God says, "And I will cast you out of My presence, just as I have cast out all your brothers, all the descendants of Ephraim." (Jeremiah 7:15). It's a heavy line. He's talking about being cast out of His presence.

The king isn't part of this warning. God says, "And I will cast you out of My presence, just as I have cast out all your brothers, all the descendants of Ephraim." (Jeremiah 7:15). This one's a heavy verse, and it's about the people themselves.
